rv.q: What's remarkable is how "The Book of Mormon" still manages to poke fun at organized religion, colonialism, and even musical theater form itself without feeling stale.
This send-up of the notorious religion remains the best ticket in town—clever, nuanced, and, surprisingly, sweet in ways newcomers might not expect.
"The Book of Mormon" is offensive, insensitive, raunchy and absolutely hilarious.
In the 21st century, the show remains wonderfully riotous, relevant, resonant and irreverent.
"The Book of Mormon" is still delivering side-splitting hilarity with its impeccable blend of catchy songs, biting satire, and nothing-is-off-limits humor.
I can't remember the last time I laughed this hard in a theater.
Fifteen years after its Broadway debut, The Book of Mormon remains one of the funniest musicals ever written.
It's also one of the funniest musicals ever, making it a must-see show.
The Book of Mormon has still got it. This is the third time a national tour of this show has stopped in Grand Rapids and it's as funny, lewd, smart, and delightful as ever.
This production manages to strike the perfect balance.
And Mormon , thousands of performances in, is still really funny.

If you're at all curious about the show, this is a great cast to see for this tour, with a fun production, some epically hilarious moments, and a lot of well done songs — and performances that aren't just crude, but even have a touch of heart.

Credit to Trey Parker, Robert Lopez and Matt Stone for naming the elephant in the room long before anyone else, and for employing comedy to hold our feet to the fire all these years later with relentless impunity .
This cast makes it all look so fun.
I would suggest getting tickets for this bold, hilarious comedy and daring yourself to enjoy it.

The cast is great, especially understudy Rayna J. who played Nabulungi on June 2nd, her strong beautiful voice working perfectly in the goofy ballads given to her (especially “Sal Tlay Ka Siti”), balancing sincerity and satire to give her jokes the perfect landing.
The cast is full of skilled singers, like Charity Arianna (Nabulungi), as well as talented comedic actors, such as Jacob Aune (Cunningham).
I’m happy to say that it’s just as sharp, funny, and daring as the hype (honestly, at this point, it’s more like a legacy ) promised it would be.

cn.t: Critics find this irreverent musical satire still hilariously offensive 15 years later, with razor-sharp wit, catchy songs, and high-energy performances that provoke both laughter and wincing—though it's decidedly not for the easily offended.
